metadata.name: date
metadata.displayName: date - Display or set the system date and time
metadata.description: Display or set the system date and time

installation.note: date is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The date command displays or sets the system date and time. It's one of the most commonly used commands for getting timestamps, formatting dates for logs, creating time-based filenames, and scheduling operations. It supports extensive formatting options to display dates and times in virtually any format needed.
when_to_use: Format dates for log files or filenames
Set system date and time (requires root)
Format dates for reports or output

syntax.description: Display current date/time, or set system date/time. With +FORMAT, displays date in specified format. Without arguments, shows default format.

options.description: Display time described by STRING, not 'now'
options.use_case: Get dates relative to now (yesterday, tomorrow, next week) or parse date strings

options.description: Set system date and time (requires root privileges)
options.use_case: Manually set system clock, usually done by system administrators

options.description: Print or set Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
options.use_case: Work with UTC time instead of local timezone, useful for logs and coordination

options.description: Output date and time in RFC 5322 format
options.use_case: Get date in email header format, useful for scripts that generate emails
Get standardized ISO format dates, useful for APIs and data exchange

misconceptions.title: date can only show current time
misconceptions.misconception: date always shows the current system time and cannot calculate other dates
misconceptions.reality: date can calculate any date using -d option: 'yesterday', 'tomorrow', 'next week', '+5 days', etc. It's very flexible for date arithmetic.
misconceptions.tip: Use -d for relative dates: date -d 'tomorrow', date -d '+1 month', date -d 'last Monday'

misconceptions.title: Format strings work without + prefix
misconceptions.misconception: You can use format strings directly like date '%Y-%m-%d'
misconceptions.reality: Format strings must be prefixed with +: date '+%Y-%m-%d'. Without +, date tries to set the system time (and fails without -s).
misconceptions.tip: Always use + before format strings: date '+%Y-%m-%d', not date '%Y-%m-%d'

misconceptions.title: date sets timezone
misconceptions.reality: date -s sets the system clock time, not the timezone. Timezone is set separately using timedatectl or TZ environment variable.
misconceptions.tip: Use timedatectl to change timezone, date -s to set the actual time

common_pitfalls.description: Using date '%Y-%m-%d' instead of date '+%Y-%m-%d' causes errors
common_pitfalls.solution: Always prefix format strings with +. The + tells date you're providing a format, not trying to set the time.

common_pitfalls.issue: Quotes needed for format strings with spaces
common_pitfalls.description: Format strings with spaces need quoting: date '+%Y %m %d' not date +%Y %m %d
common_pitfalls.solution: Always quote format strings, especially when they contain spaces or special characters

common_pitfalls.description: date -s requires sudo/root privileges and will fail for regular users
common_pitfalls.solution: Use sudo date -s 'time' to set system time. Regular users can only read the time, not set it.

related_commands.relationship: System time management; timedatectl is the modern way to set timezone, date is for getting/formatting dates
related_commands.description: Control the system time and date (systemd)

related_commands.relationship: Calendar display; cal shows calendar, date shows current date/time
File timestamps; touch uses date formats for setting file times

best_practices: Always use + prefix for format strings: date '+%Y-%m-%d'
Quote format strings to prevent shell interpretation: date '+%Y %m %d'
Use ISO 8601 format (-I) for standardized dates in scripts and APIs
Use Unix timestamps (%s) for calculations and comparisons
Create filename-safe timestamps: date '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S' (no spaces or special chars)
Use -d for relative dates in scripts: date -d 'tomorrow', date -d '+1 week'
performance_tips: date is very fast - negligible performance impact
Format strings are processed quickly, even complex ones
For high-frequency timestamp generation, date is efficient

additional_notes.format_codes: Common format codes: %Y (year), %m (month), %d (day), %H (hour), %M (minute), %S (second), %s (Unix timestamp), %A (weekday name), %B (month name)
additional_notes.relative_dates: Supports: yesterday, tomorrow, next/last week/month/year, +N days/weeks/months, specific dates
additional_notes.timezone: Use -u for UTC, or TZ environment variable for different timezones
additional_notes.setting_time: Requires root privileges. Modern systems often use NTP for automatic time synchronization
